newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss Jews cautiously hail plan for Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss Jews cautiously hail plan for Holocaust fund.

text.p: Swiss Jewish leaders on Friday hailed a decision by the government and business elite to create a memorial fund as a goodwill gesture to Jewish groups seeking amends for Holocaust victims and their families.

The fund is part of the government's efforts to calm criticism that the neutral country cynically exploited the war, including claims Swiss banks hoarded accounts left by Holocaust victims and that the central bank bought looted Nazi gold.

"We are pleased by the initiative by the cabinet and its willingness to start a fund as a gesture of goodwill," said Rolf Bloch, head of the Swiss Jewish Federation (SIG), noting that the plan incorporated ideas his group had put forward.
"Now it is a question of pursuing the difficult task of implementation and firming things up. The SIG is ready to help if called upon," he told Reuters.
Bowing to intense pressure from world Jewish groups, Switzerland's business elite and the government agreed in principle on Thursday to create the Holocaust memorial fund.
Details remain sketchy and no amount of money has been fixed for the fund, which the government and the banks had resisted for months for fear it would be seen as an admission of guilt.

SIG general secretary Martin Rosenfeld said he believed big businesses, led by the banks, would get the fund rolling and the government would later contribute a sizeable amount to make amends for neutral Switzerland's wartime role.

The government has said it will decide on a contribution only this summer, after a panel of historians launched last month reports on Swiss gold purchases that helped finance the Nazi war machine and the country's anti-Jewish wartime immigration policy.
But Rosenfeld said there was no reason to wait.
"There are already enough reasons. You don't have to search very long for them," he said.

"I don't think it is a question of approaching this like accountants. It must be a sign of goodwill on the part of Switzerland towards Holocaust victims and the rest of the world that it is ready to take responsibility."

Rosenfeld said Credit Suisse Group chairman Rainer Gut had engineered the accord by proposing that the government, the National Bank and other banks and insurers set up a fund with more than 100 million Swiss francs ($70 million).
Rosenfeld noted that Swiss banks had taken the lead in a project that had been making slow progress in Berne, the seat of government.

"It is clear to me that businesses, especially the banks, were directly confronted with Switzerland's bad image abroad. They fear of course economic losses, especially Swiss banks with their foreign branches," he said.

"This is very clearly the reason and it is understandable. Finally after months and years the banks have seen their way clear to adopt a forward-looking strategy and do something for their image. They are doing this also in their own interest."
Zurich's liberal Tages-Anzeiger daily warned against thinking the problem of Switzerland's past would now go away.

"One point must not be forgotten in all the satisfaction over positive signals: We cannot simply buy our way out of our past," it said in a commentary. "If the fund is understood to be a public ralations move, then something is wrong." ($1=1.4260 Swiss Franc)
